description: Team Hugo is an interdisciplinary team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Driven by curiosity and open science, we leverage open space agency data to design innovative prototypes addressing critical challenges on Earth and in space.
summary: Walkback is a browser-based EVA planner for Mars that answers one question: where can an astronaut go and still get back? The user sets oxygen, suit power, daylight, a safety reserve and time at the target. The smallest limit sets the mission clock. Walkback then maps every point that can be reached with the walk home still inside the budget. It uses a slope-aware walking model, where uphill and downhill take different amounts of time. It offers three routes to a chosen target (Fastest, Safest and Science), rates each one GO, TIGHT or NO-GO, and writes step-by-step directions for the walk out and the walk back. A live EVA mode re-plans from the astronaut’s position and switches to the return directions at the turnaround point. This build runs on synthetic sample terrain shaped like a crater floor, rim and delta, and the app labels this clearly. Real HiRISE elevation data and validation against Perseverance’s traverse are the next steps.
details:
What it does: Walkback helps plan a Mars surface walk (EVA). The astronaut is limited by oxygen, suit power and daylight, and the smallest of the three sets the clock. After a safety reserve and the time spent at the target, the remaining time must cover the walk out and the walk home. Walkback shows every place that fits this budget, which we call the reach zone, instead of only drawing a path from A to B.

How it works: The terrain is a 170 × 120 elevation grid with 30 m cells. Slope is computed for every step between neighbouring cells. Walking time comes from distance and a slope-dependent pace, slower on steep and soft ground, and uphill and downhill cost different amounts of time. We run Dijkstra’s algorithm from the habitat once for the walk out and once on reversed edges for the walk home. A cell is in reach if the out time plus the back time fits the usable time. For a chosen target the app builds three routes: Fastest, Safest (stays under a comfort slope limit and avoids soft ground) and Science (detours past science targets while the trip still fits the budget). Each route is rated GO, TIGHT or NO-GO from its margin at the habitat.

Directions and live mode: Each route is turned into legs with compass heading, distance, slope, time and budget left, for both the outbound and the return trip. A destination check says whether the target is verified, tight, outside the budget or unreachable, and suggests the nearest reachable point and a fix. In live EVA mode the astronaut moves along the route, consumables only go down, the plan is recomputed from the current position, and the directions switch to Return at the turnaround point.

Benefits and impact: Crew and mission planners get a clear answer to “how far is too far”, with the reasoning shown. Every number comes from the planner’s own calculations, and the app separates derived, measured and assumed values.

Tools: React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS. The planner is plain TypeScript with no backend and no AI model at runtime. We built it with Google AI Studio and Claude, hosted the code on GitHub and deployed it on Vercel.

Data and honesty: This version uses synthetic sample terrain shaped like a crater floor, rim and delta, and the map labels it as not real Mars data. Walking pace, slope limits, soft-ground slowdown and reserve are assumptions, not NASA operating limits. The tool is not for real mission use.

What we considered: Return time assumes the astronaut retraces the outbound path. We chose physical limits (slope and time budgets) over arbitrary risk scores, so each result can be explained.

Next steps: Replace the sample grid with HiRISE elevation data of Jezero Crater, validate the planner against Perseverance’s traverse, add line-of-sight analysis for communication dead zones, and use MEDA weather data for timing.

AI use: Claude (Anthropic) helped plan the idea, draft the slides and write build prompts. Gemini in Google AI Studio generated and edited the app code. The team directed the work, reviewed and tested the result. The cover illustration in the slides was drawn with AI and is labelled as AI-generated. No AI-generated video or audio was used.

Source code: https://github.com/krushna3042/Walkback-EVA
